title-group.article-title: Targeted microwave ablation of localised prostate cancer (VIOLETTE trial): a prospective multicentre study

sec.title: Objective
sec.p: To assess the oncological outcomes of targeted microwave ablation (TMA) using organ‐based tracking (OBT) Fusion® via KOELIS Trinity® (KOELIS, Meylan, France) in men with intermediate‐risk prostate cancer (PCa): the VIOLETTE trial (ClinicalTrials.gov identifier: NCT04582656)

sec.title: Patients and Method
sec.p: In this prospective phase II, multicentre European study, men with a prostate‐specific antigen (PSA) level <20 ng/mL, a single magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)‐visible lesion ≤15 mm, International Society of Urological Pathology (ISUP) Grade Group 2 on MRI‐targeted biopsy, and clinical T stage ≤2, were enrolled. The microwave applicator was placed using OBT Fusion guidance, either transperineally or transrectally. The primary endpoint was the absence of clinically significant PCa (csPCa), defined as ISUP Grade Group ≥2, within the treated area at 12 months. Secondary endpoints included safety, functional outcomes using validated measures, and the need for subsequent radical treatment.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: A total of 76 patients were treated across six centres with 66 (87%) completing the 12‐month follow‐up. At 6 months, six patients had csPCa after positive MRI control, including four within the treated area. At 12 months, csPCa was detected in 15 additional patients, including nine in‐field recurrences, yielding an 81% in‐field csPCa‐free rate. Five serious adverse events in three patients were reported. Sexual (−2.5 points; P < 0.001) and ejaculatory (−1 points; P < 0.001) scores decreased significantly, whereas urinary function remained stable. Radical treatment was required in four (5.2%) patients at 12 months.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: Targeted microwave ablation using OBT Fusion technology appears to be a safe and effective focal therapy procedure for localised intermediate‐risk PCa. The VIOLETTE trial achieved its primary endpoint, with 81% patients free of in‐field csPCa at 12 months.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Focal therapy (FT) has gained interest in recent years in patients with localised clinically significant prostate cancer (csPCa) [1]. This potential alternative to whole‐gland therapy aims at mitigating adverse impacts on sexual, urinary and bowel function [2], as well as to decrease overtreatment in patients presenting with earlier stage and smaller size cancers [3]. Various sources of energy have been employed to date to ablate the index tumour, but, according to current guidelines, this treatment strategy remains experimental due to the lack of long‐term oncological data [1, 4, 5, 6].

Targeted microwave ablation (TMA) is a novel needle‐based FT modality associating a thermo‐ablative energy (microwaves [MWs]) with a real‐time guidance system using organ‐based tracking (OBT) Fusion® technology (KOELIS, Meylan, France) combined with MRI‐ultrasonography fusion (KOELIS Trinity®) [7, 8]. The latter is used at the time of diagnosis to precisely guide prostate biopsy to the target MRI lesion and map the rest of the biopsies sampling in a three‐dimensional (3D) cartography [9]. Later on, in appropriately selected patients, the OBT fusion system is used to recall 3D‐positive biopsy locations and MRI lesions, in order to define ablation margins. Multiple consecutive single‐needle MW ablations are doable to sculpt the MRI lesion together with a margin embedding positive targeted biopsies [10].

In addition to the ability to adapt precisely to the shape of the tumour, a potential distinct advantage of TMA resides in the comprehensive strategy of cancer characterisation, treatment and follow‐up biopsies using the same image guidance system. Also, the MW generator is small and transportable, and only one needle is needed for a complete treatment. Four preliminary studies suggested the feasibility and precision of the technique, using the transrectal [11, 12] or transperineal [13, 14] approach. We conducted a European prospective phase II multicentric trial to assess the oncological value of TMA in patients with intermediate‐risk localised PCa.

sec.title: Study Characteristics and Endpoints
sec.p: This prospective phase II interventional study (VIOLETTE trial) was approved by the French Committee for Medical and Health Ethics and registered on ClinicalTrial.gov (NCT04582656).

Its primary objective consisted in assessing the treatment efficacy, with treatment success defined according to a Delphi consensus [15] as the absence of International Society of Urological Pathology (ISUP) Grade Group ≥2 cancer remaining in the treated area, measured with MRI‐targeted and systematic biopsies performed 12 months after TMA, and centralised histological analysis of biopsy specimen.

Secondary objectives and endpoints were: (i) intra‐ and postoperative outcomes, including safety, assessed with prostatic MRI 7 days after procedure, adverse events (AEs) reporting and pain score evaluation; (ii) urinary and sexual outcomes; (iii) PSA kinetics; and (iv) treatment zone shape on MRI at Day 7, and at 6 and 12 months.

sec.title: Eligibility Criteria
sec.p: Inclusion criteria were: (i) age between 45 and 80 years; (ii) patients with favourable intermediate‐risk PCa, (iii) PSA level <20 ng/mL, and (iv) a unique MRI‐visible tumour focus characterised on targeted biopsies as Gleason score 3 + 4 or ISUP Grade Group 2, and defined as csPCa. We excluded patients (i) harbouring a tumour focus with a largest axis >15 mm, (ii) a tumour focus of ISUP Grade Group >2, or (iii) closer than 5 mm from the rectum or the far apex, as well as (iv) patients with more than ISUP Grade Group 1 cancer on systematic biopsies.

sec.title: Intervention
sec.p: All procedures are performed under general anaesthesia and/or conscious intravenous sedation. The technique was described previously [11, 12, 13, 14]. Urethral catheterisation is performed on a case‐by‐case basis to locate the urethra during the procedure. The ultrasound probe is inserted transrectally and held with a mechanical arm (Steady Pro™, KOELIS). Ultrasound‐MRI image fusion is performed with OBT‐fusion using the KOELIS Trinity system [8, 16]. The contours of the MRI visible tumour are delineated manually by the investigator on the software. A treatment margin (in mm) is then selected by the investigator and applied by the software.

The MW ablation is provided by the TATO™ generator (Biomedical, Firenze, Italy), using a single 17‐G needle inserted into the index lesion via transperineal approach, or using a 18‐G needle via transrectal approach, according to the investigator's choice of approach. Duration and power of MW application are directly related to the olive‐shaped ablation size and are set according to predictive ablation charts. Surrounding structures like urethra and rectum can be depicted in the 3D environment to help safe ablation positioning. Each setting can be displayed and the planned ablations placed in 3D ultrasound on the KOELIS Trinity system, until the lesion is satisfactorily covered by ablations, including a lesion‐shaped margin drawn around it. The evaluation of the intervention quality can be instantly assessed by the percentage of target coverage in the treated area.

sec.title: Follow‐Up
sec.p: All patients were reviewed at Day 7 and at 1, 3, 6, 9 and 12 months after surgery. Total PSA was collected at 3, 6 and 12 months. The IPSS, five‐item version of the International Index of Erectile Function (IIEF‐5) and Male Sexual Health Questionnaire for Ejaculatory Dysfunction (MSHQ‐EjD) self‐administered questionnaires were collected at each visit. A multiparametric prostate MRI was performed at Day 7, and at 6 and 12 months, and prostate volume was calculated at these timepoints. The extent of necrosis at Day 7 was evaluated with T1‐contrast‐enhanced weighted sequences. Prostate re‐biopsy was taken at 6 months only in case of untreated or relapsing tumour suspicion on MRI and performed at 12 months for all patients. AEs were reported using the Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events (CTCAE) version 5.0 and Clavien–Dindo classification.

sec.title: Statistical Analysis
sec.p: A sample size of 65 patients provides the ability to calculate a two‐sided 95% exact binomial CI for an 80% efficacy rate with a CI that is ± 10.3% (80% ± 10.3%), i.e., 69.7–90.3%. Taking into account a 10% dropped out patient rate, the final sample size was 76 treated patients to obtain at least 65 patients with a 12‐month primary endpoint evaluation.

Statistical analyses were performed using R version 4.4.2 (2024‐10‐31 ucrt; R Foundation for Statistical Computing, Vienna, Austria). All quantitative data were described as median and interquartile range (IQR). All qualitative data were described as numbers and proportions.

The Clopper–Pearson 95% CI was used to describe the primary effectiveness endpoint, the proportion of patients with a negative in‐field biopsy. Univariate logistic regression analyses were conducted to evaluate the association between endpoint and covariates, including inclusion rank, PSA level, PSA density, prostate volume, lesion largest axis, Prostate Imaging‐Reporting and Data System (PI‐RADS) score, percentage Grade 4, treatment margin, and presence of necrosis on prostate MRI at 7 days postoperatively.

sec.title: Patients’ Characteristics, Procedure and Perioperative Details
sec.p: Between December 2021 and August 2024, 80 patients were enrolled in 6 centres after fully informed consent. Finally, 76 eligible patients were treated with TMA (Fig. 1, flow chart). Demographics and disease characteristics are summarised in Table 1.

sec.p: In all, 69 (91%) patients were treated in an ambulatory setting, 51 (67%) and 25 (33%) under general anaesthesia or conscious intravenous sedation, respectively. Intraoperative outcomes are summarised in Table 2. Total median (IQR) duration of procedure was 51 (42–62) min, including 10 (8–13) min of MW ablation for an average of three ablations per patient allowing to cover 100% (100–100%) of the pre‐defined target on the KOELIS Trinity system. In all, 65 patients (86%) recovered spontaneous voiding after treatment and were discharged without any catheter. The median postoperative pain level was considered by patients as ≤2 on a 0–10 visual analogue scale for 70 (93%) of them.

sec.p: At 7 days after the procedure, the volume of non‐vascularised prostatic tissue on dynamic contrast‐enhanced MRI was visible in 73 (96%) patients, with a median (IQR) necrosis volume of 6 (4–8) mL. For the 11 patients with a catheter at discharge, it was removed within a median (IQR) of 4 (4–5) days.

sec.title: Follow‐Up and Oncological Results
sec.p: Three patients dropped out before the 6‐month follow‐up (Fig. 1), leaving 73 patients available for the 6‐month analysis. One patient had a TURP, another withdrew his consent and was addressed for brachytherapy, and one dropped out following myocardial infarction.

The 6‐month prostate MRI showed no evidence of suspicious in‐field image in 64/73 (88%) patients. Seven patients underwent early biopsy control. Of them, four showed early in‐field treatment failure with evidence of ISUP Grade Group 2 cancer on targeted biopsies (Table 3), and two others showed evidence of outfield ISUP Grade group 2 cancers. These patients exited the study. Between the 6‐ and 12‐month follow up, one patient retracted his consent for personal reasons and quit the study, leaving 66 patients for the 12‐month MRI follow‐up. The 12‐month MRI did not show any suspicion of in‐field residual tumour in 48/66 (87%) patients. Two patients showing non‐suspicious MRI did not undergo the 12‐month biopsy and existed the study earlier, due to consent retrieval (personal reasons) and cardiac arrythmia, respectively. The 12‐month biopsies showed in‐field csPCa in nine of 64 (14%) patients. The primary efficacy endpoint was therefore evaluated in 68 patients (including four patients at 6 months and 64 at 12 months) demonstrating a rate of negative in‐field biopsy for csPCa of 81% (55/68; 95% CI 0.69–0.89) after 12 months. The rate of cancer‐negative in‐field biopsies was of 59% (40/68; 95% CI 0.48–0.72). Out‐field biopsy control at 12‐months showed csPCa in six patients, resulting in a total of eight of the 66 evaluable patients with an out‐field cancer progression after the 12‐month follow up. Single logistic regression analysis did not show any patient or treatment‐related factors associated with in‐field csPCa at 12 months.

sec.title: Prostate‐Specific Antigen Kinetics and Prostate Volume
sec.p: At 12 months, the median (IQR) PSA level was 4.35 (2.87–7.05) ng/mL, showing a median (IQR) decrease of −2.4 (−4.42 to 0.37) ng/mL, representing a 38% PSA level decrease after TMA. The median (IQR) PSA nadir was 3.3 (1.7–5.5) ng/mL, and median (IQR) time to PSA nadir was 3.1 (2.3–5.9) months. The median (IQR) prostate volume was 41 (29–59) mL at 12 months, showing a 10% decrease. The median (IQR) PSA density decreased from 0.18 (0.1–0.24) ng/mL2 at baseline to 0.10 (0.07–0.14) ng/mL2 at 12 months showing a 44% reduction. (Fig. 2).

caption.p: Evolution of total PSA level, prostate volume, and PSA density. M1, Month 1; M3, Month 3; M6, Month 6; M9, Month 9; M12, Month 12.

sec.title: Re‐treatment
sec.p: One patient had brachytherapy before the 6‐month follow up. The two patients with an out‐field cancer progression on 6‐month biopsy had a radical treatment. Of the four patients with residual in‐field significant disease at 6 months, two had a radical treatment, one had an additional TMA, and one remained on active surveillance. The rate of radical treatment was four of 76 (5.2%) at 12 months.

sec.title: Functional Outcomes
sec.p: Figure 3 summarises the evolution of urinary and sexual outcomes. There was no difference in the IPSS between baseline and the 12‐month follow up. We observed a deterioration of erectile function at 12 months, with a median decrease of 2.5 points in IIEF‐5 score (P < 0.001). In all, 33/76 (43%) vs 18/64 (28%) patients reported an IIEF‐5 score of ≥21 points (erectile function considered as normal) at baseline and 12 months, respectively. Ejaculatory function showed also a slight but significant decrease (median MSHQ‐EjD score decrease of 1 point, P < 0.001), but without any difference in related bother.

caption.p: Urinary and sexual functional outcomes after TMA. D7, Day 7; M1, Month 1; M6, Month 6; M12, Month 12.

sec.title: Safety
sec.p: Overall, 44 (58%) patients experienced 88 AEs. Of them, 76 were considered to be at least possibly related to the procedure for 41 patients including 56 CTCAE Grade 1 (74%), 17 Grade 2 (22%), and 3 Grade 3 (4%). Using the Clavien–Dindo classification, these 76 postoperative complications were considered Grade I, II, and IIIb in 56 (74%), 19 (25%), and one (1%) case, respectively. Most of AEs (56 [74%]) were observed in the immediate postoperative period of 1 month. The most common AEs (>10% of the patients) included urinary retention (12%, including two CTCAE Grade 3), haematuria (11%), dysuria (11%), urinary discomfort (14%), and haematospermia (13%). The median (IQR) resolution delay for AEs was 25 (7–54) days.

Six patients experienced nine serious AEs (SAEs). Of them, five were at least possibly related to the procedure for three patients: one patient experienced prostatitis with acute urinary retention 2 days after the procedure, requiring hospital admission. A second patient experienced urinary retention 3 days after the procedure, requiring Foley catheter placement and eventually TURP 1 month later. Another patient experienced acute urinary retention and was hospitalised for 1 day for drainage and monitoring. Three other patients experienced four SAEs unrelated to the procedure. Two of them myocardial infarction and arrythmia, respectively, and exited earlier the study. The third patient had a hip surgical repair complicated with sepsis but completed his follow up.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: The VIOLETTE trial represents the first European multicentric phase II evaluation of OBT‐guided TMA in men with intermediate‐risk PCa harbouring a single ISUP Grade 2 index tumour. In this Idea, Development, Exploration, Assessment, Long‐term follow‐up (IDEAL) phase IIb evaluation, the primary endpoint regards effectiveness, according to a Delphi consensus [15]. We demonstrated an 81% negative in‐field biopsy rate for csPCa at 12 months. Such an individual endpoint, however, should always be considered in the light of the various underlying criteria that support FT success or failure.

There are three acknowledged origins for early oncological failure after PCa FT [15]: ablation failure, meaning the energy used did not allow appropriate tissue destruction in the intended treated zone; targeting failure, related to a lack of precision in ablation guidance within the intended treated zone, including margins; and last but not least, disease underestimation at the time of patient selection, which leads to an overall failure of the entire strategy. The first two causes of failure (energy and targeting) are difficult to evaluate separately in the present study. However, regarding MW effectiveness, a previous ‘ablate and resect’ study [12] showed no evidence of residual viable tissue in the prostatic area where MW thermo‐ablation was applied, underlining the validity of this ablative therapeutic approach. In the VIOLETTE trial, the choice in the treatment margins applied, the number and duration of each MW ablation was left to each investigator's judgement according to clinical practice. Nevertheless, because all patients received at least two MW applications, some tumour areas were treated several times, according to the treatment planning.

In addition, regarding OBT fusion targeting accuracy, evidence has been published on a baseline 3D image registration error of <1 mm [17] and on a final average target registration error of <3 mm [18, 19], which is consistent with the principle of ablating an anatomical volume in a radial manner starting from the centre of the target. Moreover, a unique and key advantage of OBT fusion remains its ability (known as ‘second look fusion’) to precisely recall the previously recorded 3D mapping of biopsy cores, MRI lesions, MW ablations, referenced to the patient's prostate, for the purpose of post‐biopsy treatment or post‐treatment biopsy.

The third cause of failure highlights the challenges and limitations of cancer characterisation before proposing active surveillance or FT. Advances in combined MRI and positron emission tomography, as well as biomarkers, will hopefully decrease patient misclassification in the near future.

In the present evaluation, baseline biopsies, treatment targeting, and control biopsies were performed using the same guidance system (KOELIS Trinity OBT fusion). The precise location of baseline targeted biopsies and ablation volume were recorded in the KOELIS Trinity system and recalled 1 year later to optimise the targeting of control biopsies, especially in those patients who did not show any evidence of residual tumour on the 12‐month MRI (62 patients). Because of target tissues shrinkage and unpredictable change in prostate shape, it may be challenging to biopsy a treated zone that may have shifted or disappeared altogether. For that reason, despite the precise ‘second look fusion’ targeting feature we currently used, we think that we probably increased our apparent rate of in‐field cancer detection. Nevertheless, this methodology permitted to get closer to the true prevalence of residual in‐field tumour. Other potential advantages of using the same guidance system for diagnosis, treatment and follow up biopsies are to optimise the learning curve in using the system, decrease the carbon footprint in operating rooms as well as costs.

Over the past 5 years, FT has been studied for eight different energy sources, mostly in single‐arm IDEAL phase I and II studies [1]. Although a first randomised controlled trial was performed to evaluate photodynamic therapy, the population studied was solely comprised of men with ISUP Grade Group 1 cancer, therefore reducing the clinical relevance of the oncological results [20]. Focal high‐intensity focused ultrasound (HIFU) has been the most evaluated technique in prospective development studies. The heterogeneity in the populations studied (low to high staged disease), ablation modalities (from focal to hemi‐ablation and beyond), guidance used (with TRUS alone or MRI‐TRUS fusion), as well as that of biopsy techniques for oncological evaluation (saturation, template, or targeted biopsies), makes the clinical interpretation of ‘in‐field oncological control’ challenging. According to a recent systematic review [1], nine of the 17 studies evaluating focal, zonal or hemi‐ablation using HIFU (without associated TURP) reported on csPCa in the treated area at 6–12 months, with a median (range) failure rate of 15.4% (0–21.8%). More recently results were published the of the PRESERVE trial (NCT04972097; IDEAL Stage IIb) evaluating irreversible electroporation (IRE) in patients with intermediate‐risk localised PCa. The authors reported a 16% in‐field csPCa rate at 12 months [21]. This rate increased to 21% when including ISUP Grade Group 1 cancers. However, it is currently consensually accepted that residual in‐field ISUP Grade Group 1 disease should not be considered as treatment failures because they do not need additional treatment [15, 22, 23].

Although our multivariate analysis did not show any patient or treatment‐related factor associated with in‐field treatment failure, it seems reasonable to suggest that treatment extension and margins remain key points to reach an optimal oncological control. However, the latter has to be balanced with safety. An extension of the necrosis area beyond the target zone may potentially result in AEs, especially if the treatment zone is located close to the rectal wall, to the urethra or to the neurovascular bundles. Even though recto prostatic fistula is rare after FT, the risk is real for posterior tumours and cases have been reported in the recent literature [1, 21]. According to recent reviews [1, 4], urinary incontinence and erectile dysfunction are reported between 0% and 10% depending on studies [24, 25, 26]. UTI and urinary retention are by far the most common Grade 2 and 3 complications after HIFU, cryotherapy and IRE. In the present study, most of AEs were related to dysuria, haematuria and urinary frequency; amongst urinary retention all but one resolved spontaneously after a few days of bladder drainage. One patient showed a prostate volume of 80 mL and a preoperative IPSS of 18 points. He eventually underwent TURP, with satisfactory outcomes.

The total PSA level is relevant for patient follow‐up during active surveillance but may be much less reliable after any FT [4, 22]. In the latter, PSA kinetics may not reflect directly the efficacy of treatment, but rather the reduction in prostate size following tissue ablation. In our evaluation, a new estimation of prostate volume was performed at 6 and 12 months based on MRI. Therefore, calculating PSA density may compensate a possible bias for each patient.

Our study is limited by several factors, including the absence of comparator and short follow‐up of only 12 months, which is insufficient to draw strong conclusions on long‐term cancer control. However, this drawback is common in phase II FT evaluations. At least two randomised trials evaluating focal HIFU vs radical prostatectomy are ongoing, in Norway (FARP study; NCT03668652) and in France (EMERHIT study; NCT05710861) and will hopefully bring strong oncological data to support FT strategy. Furthermore, final biopsy compliance was incomplete (three patients) and may have induced bias. Some factors also brought heterogeneity between centres and may have affected our results. These include the choice between the transrectal or transperineal approach, as well as the use of framing biopsies at baseline, that was left to the investigator's choice. Last but not least, most centres had no initial experience in TMA at study initiation. However, the small number of patients did not allow any evaluation of the learning curve. Nonetheless, our work stands as the first multicentric evaluation of this innovative OBT‐guided FT.

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: The VIOLETTE trial met its primary endpoint with 81% patients free of in‐field csPCa at 12 months. TMA reveals itself as an ambulatory, safe and effective needle‐based FT with positive short‐term oncological and functional outcomes.
